assertions.description: AbortController.abort() takes an arbitrary reason and stores it on the signal. This is the mechanism the whole feature forwards.
With no argument the platform supplies an AbortError DOMException, so signal.reason is never undefined on an aborted signal.
The pre-existing behaviour: aborting an in-flight request rejects the fetch promise with the reason itself.

The change itself: after the Response exists, aborting must reject body-reading methods with the SAME reason rather than a substituted AbortError. Before Chrome 154 this rejected with a generic DOMException and the reason was lost.
assertions.test: (async()=>{const c=new AbortController();const reason={code:'CONF_BODY'};let r;try{r=await fetch('/public/media/jpeg-xl/source.png?conf='+Math.floor(performance.now()),{signal:c.signal});}catch(e){return false;}c.abort(reason);try{await r.text();return false;}catch(e){return e===reason;}})()

assertions.description: The body's ReadableStream must surface the reason too. A streaming reader is where long downloads spend their time, so this is the site that matters most in practice.
assertions.test: (async()=>{const c=new AbortController();const reason={code:'CONF_STREAM'};let r;try{r=await fetch('/public/media/jpeg-xl/source.png?conf='+Math.floor(performance.now()),{signal:c.signal});}catch(e){return false;}c.abort(reason);try{const rd=r.body.getReader();for(;;){const {done}=await rd.read();if(done)break;}return false;}catch(e){return e===reason;}})()

assertions.description: AbortSignal.any() composes a user controller with a deadline, which is the wiring that makes distinguishing the two causes necessary in the first place.
AbortSignal.timeout() aborts with a TimeoutError DOMException, not an AbortError — which is what lets a handler tell a deadline from a cancellation by name alone.
